title: By agreeing to disarm, Hamas is trying to call Israel’s bluff in Gaza
gist: Chatham House argues that Hamas's public acceptance of Trump's decommissioning roadmap is a tactical move by new leader Khalil al-Hayya to shift the burden of intransigence onto Israel, whose control of Gaza has grown from ~53 per cent in October 2025 to nearly 70 per cent while the Board of Peace focused solely on disarmament. Both sides are expected to stall on sequencing rather than commit, leaving implementation dependent on Trump's uncertain personal follow-through.

insights.claim: Since the October 2025 Gaza ceasefire, the Board of Peace has made Hamas's disarmament the sole gate to every other element of Trump's 20-point plan, which has functionally removed Israeli withdrawal from the negotiating agenda.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Any headline about 'progress on disarmament' should be read as a delay mechanism for withdrawal, not a step toward de-escalation — the reconstruction and reopening trade stays deferred.
insights.quote: Most crucially, the emphasis on disarmament has precluded any discussion of Israel’s withdrawal from Gaza.
insights.locator: Since the Gaza ceasefire came into effect

insights.claim: Israeli territorial control of Gaza has expanded from about 53 per cent in October 2025, delineated by the 'Yellow Line', to nearly 70 per cent as of August 2026 — an increase that occurred during rather than before the ceasefire.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The ceasefire has been a vehicle for Israeli territorial consolidation; the practical baseline for any 'withdrawal' talk is now far worse for Hamas than the October line.
insights.quote: from about 53 per cent of Gaza in October (delineated by the so-called ‘Yellow Line’) to nearly 70 per cent today

insights.claim: Three concrete deliverables remain blocked behind the disarmament question in Gaza: entry of the technocratic National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), deployment of an International Stabilization Force (ISF), and the start of reconstruction.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Watch NCAG entry and ISF deployment as the only hard, observable milestones — reconstruction contracting and regional infrastructure exposure cannot begin before them.
insights.locator: These include the entry into Gaza of the technocratic

insights.claim: Hamas's agreement to Trump's disarmament plan is read as a pragmatic manoeuvre by new leader Khalil al-Hayya to keep the group inside the conversation on Gaza's future and shift the onus of intransigence onto Israel, not as a genuine intent to hand over weapons.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Treat the acceptance as a diplomatic positioning trade, not a disarmament event — the follow-through gap is where headlines will reverse.
insights.quote: Agreeing to Trump’s plan is likely a pragmatic move by new Hamas leader Khalil al-Hayya.
insights.locator: Dragging out the process also suits Hamas

insights.claim: Hamas's acceptance of the disarmament roadmap could generate the first genuine external pressure on Israel over Gaza in months, reversing a dynamic in which only Hamas faced demands.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The key variable to monitor is whether Washington converts rhetorical pressure into leverage on Israel — that is the only realistic catalyst for a de-escalation repricing.
insights.quote: By essentially calling Israel’s bluff, Hamas’s move could potentially put external pressure on Israel in Gaza for the first time in months.
insights.locator: President Trump’s recent announcement that Hamas has agreed

insights.claim: Benjamin Netanyahu is expected to stretch out negotiations on Gaza because US pressure to withdraw ahead of October's Israeli elections would cost him his voter base, making any public concession to Hamas politically prohibitive before the vote.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: October's Israeli election is the binding constraint — expect no substantive withdrawal timeline before it, and price any pre-election 'breakthrough' as theatre.
insights.quote: the last thing he wants as he goes into October’s elections is US pressure to withdraw from Gaza
insights.locator: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu will likely seek

insights.claim: Right-wing Israeli ministers have already announced plans for new settlements inside Gaza, moving in the opposite direction from the withdrawal contemplated by Trump's roadmap.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Settlement announcements are the cleanest tell that Israeli coalition politics is committed to permanence in Gaza, raising the tail risk of ceasefire collapse.
insights.locator: Far from accepting Israel’s withdrawal from the enclave

insights.claim: The core structural blockage in Gaza is mirrored sequencing: Israel demands full Hamas disarmament before any withdrawal, while Hamas demands Israeli withdrawal before decommissioning weapons — the same impasse that has defeated previous agreements.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Use 'who moves first' as the single diagnostic for whether any new Gaza announcement is real; absent a first-mover mechanism, the deal is non-operational.
insights.quote: Israel will likely require full Hamas disarmament before withdrawal, while Hamas will likely insist on Israeli withdrawal before decommissioning weapons.
insights.locator: Indeed, both actors will likely double down on sequencing demands

insights.claim: Israel has reportedly told the Board of Peace it reserves the right to strike areas due to be handed over to the International Stabilization Force, and objected to Qatar and Turkey — the central mediators of the Hamas agreement — participating in future verification stages.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A reserved right to strike ISF-designated zones means troop-contributing countries face direct risk, which will slow or shrink any stabilization force deployment.
insights.locator: Israel reportedly insisted to the Board of Peace

insights.claim: Israel has demanded that Hamas's confiscated weapons be destroyed rather than stored, and Hamas has explicitly rejected that demand — an unresolved technical detail that alone can stall the whole roadmap.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Destruction-versus-storage is the kind of granular disagreement that quietly kills implementation while headlines still read 'agreement reached'.
insights.locator: It also reportedly demanded that Hamas’s weapons be destroyed

insights.claim: Hamas has made its own steps conditional on Israel ending all forms of aggression, withdrawing to the October ceasefire's 'Yellow Line', facilitating entry of the ISF and NCAG, and meeting humanitarian aid obligations — a bundle Israel has shown no sign of accepting.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Hamas's conditions require Israel to give back roughly 17 percentage points of Gaza territory it has gained — a demand with effectively zero near-term probability.
insights.locator: It has stated that its moves will be contingent

insights.claim: US and Board of Peace officials describe the roadmap as 'zero trust', proceeding only on externally verified steps, but even a fully reciprocal process still requires one party to take the first step — a gap the design does not resolve.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: A verification-only architecture without a first-mover mechanism predicts stalemate by construction, regardless of how the parties are described publicly.
insights.quote: But even reciprocal processes require one side to take the first step.

themes.theme: Language as substance: decommissioning, not disarmament

insights.claim: The word 'disarmament' does not appear anywhere in Trump's Gaza roadmap, which instead uses 'decommissioning' modelled in part on Northern Ireland's process, and Hamas has deliberately avoided the vocabulary of disarmament or surrender.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: The gap between what officials say ('disarmament') and what the document says ('decommissioning') is the built-in ambiguity both sides will exploit to claim compliance without acting.
insights.quote: the term ‘disarmament’ does not appear anywhere in Trump’s roadmap, relying instead on ‘decommissioning,’ modelled in part on Northern Ireland’s process
insights.locator: Hamas has also rejected Israeli demands that weapons be destroyed

insights.claim: The Palestinian statehood question is embedded in the plan only indirectly — Article 8 of the disarmament plan points to remaining commitments under the Sharm el Sheikh Protocol, whose Point 19 references a credible pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood — which Netanyahu has fully rejected and Hamas will insist on.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Full decommissioning is tied to a statehood clause the Israeli PM has already rejected outright, meaning the roadmap contains an irreducible contradiction at its endpoint.
insights.quote: Netanyahu has fully rejected the notion of Palestinian statehood, while Hamas will insist upon it.
insights.locator: Furthermore, Hamas will likely resist full decommissioning

themes.theme: Enforcement gap and Trump follow-through risk

insights.claim: Egypt, Turkey and Qatar had enough leverage to get Hamas to publicly accept the agreement but will have far less to make it implement, because they have no physical presence on the ground in Gaza to enforce commitments or provide security guarantees.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Mediator leverage peaks at the announcement and decays afterwards — the acceptance headline is the high-water mark unless a force is physically deployed.
insights.locator: For Hamas, the mediating efforts of Egypt, Turkey, and Qatar

insights.claim: It remains unclear whether the US, and by extension the Board of Peace, will impose substantive pressure on Israel even to discuss withdrawal, making Washington's willingness the single decisive variable in the process.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Track concrete US pressure signals on Israel rather than statements about Hamas — the former is the only lever that can break the stalemate.
insights.locator: On the Israeli side, it remains unclear the extent

insights.claim: The disarmament roadmap risks becoming another casualty of a pattern in which a numbered plan is launched with fanfare and then flounders for lack of the sustained operational work needed to implement it.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Base rate for these announcements is decay, not delivery; fade the initial headline move in regional risk assets unless operational milestones appear.
insights.quote: in which a numbered plan is released with bravado, but then flounders without the long, arduous subsequent work required to make it operational
insights.locator: First is the question of Trump’s personal commitment

insights.claim: The most likely near-term outcome is that both Israel and Hamas tell the Board of Peace some semblance of what it wants to hear while avoiding real commitments by objecting to the myriad thorny implementation details.
insights.speaker: Chatham House
insights.so_what: Expect performative compliance rather than rupture or resolution — a low-volatility, unresolved stalemate is the modal path into and past October.
insights.quote: It is more likely that both sides will buy time by telling the Board of Peace at least some semblance of what it wants to hear.
